title_en: Why Building a Crosswalk in LA Is Kafkaesque
title_zh: 在 LA 建一个人行横道为何如此'卡夫卡'：对话 Bill McBride（Calculated Risk）与 Zach Lasry（The Western Company）
subtitle_zh: Odd Lots 洛杉矶现场，两位嘉宾聊房地产、分区法规与建人行横道的荒诞。
description: Why Building a Crosswalk in LA Is Kafkaesque

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios Podcasts Radio News.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。播客。电台。新闻。

turns.en: Music Hello, and welcome to another live episode of the Odd Lots podcast.
turns.zh: （音乐）大家好，欢迎来到 Odd Lots 播客的又一期现场节目。

turns.en: I'm Joe Wiesenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: So we're here at the Vermont Theater in Hollywood. And of course, you talk about Hollywood, but you also have to talk about the real estate industry. We know this has always been a hub of booming real estate industry. But what do the changes in economic development and the housing market, how does it manifest itself here?
turns.zh: 我们现在是在 Hollywood 的 Vermont Theater。说到 Hollywood，你当然绕不开房地产行业。我们知道这里一直是房地产蓬勃发展的重镇。但经济发展和住房市场的这些变化，在这里具体是怎么体现出来的呢？

turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: So we have a real treat for you.
turns.zh: 今天我们给大家准备了一份大餐。

turns.en: We're going to be speaking to an absolute legend in the world of residential real estate, someone who actually called the subprime bubble before 2008, and maybe even more importantly, called the bottom of the housing market after 2008. And then we're also going to be speaking to a relative newcomer in the world of commercial property, someone who's doing new things in L.A. and trying to develop basically a new neighborhood.
turns.zh: 我们要对话的是住宅房地产领域的一位绝对的传奇人物，他在 2008 年之前就预判到了次贷泡沫（subprime bubble），也许更重要的是，还在 2008 年之后抄到了住房市场的底部。然后我们还要对话一位商业地产领域的相对新人，他正在 L.A. 做一些新东西，基本上是想开发出一个全新的街区。

turns.en: So enjoy our conversation with the legend Bill McBride of Calculated Risk, as well as Zach Lazzari, real estate developer, founder.
turns.zh: 那就来欣赏我们与传奇人物、Calculated Risk 的 Bill McBride，以及房地产开发商、创始人 Zach Lasry 的对话吧。

turns.en: Of The Western Company. Thank you both so much. Zach, what do you what do you do? What's your job?
turns.zh: The Western Company 的创始人。非常感谢你们两位。Zach，你是做什么的？你的工作是什么？

turns.en: I'm a real estate professional.
turns.zh: 我是一名房地产专业人士（real estate professional）。

turns.en: Okay, what does that mean?
turns.zh: 好，那是什么意思？

turns.en: Because there are a lot of people who could say those words.
turns.zh: 因为很多人都能说出这几个字。

turns.en: So my goal with the Western Company, the goal that we have is that being able to say I'm a real estate professional is more exciting than it normally is. So I come from a theater and acting background. And what I noticed was the developments that I was seeing in Los Angeles moved here in about 2014.
turns.zh: 所以我在 The Western Company 的目标，我们公司的目标，就是让'我是一名房地产专业人士'这句话说出来比平时更让人兴奋。我是戏剧和表演出身。我注意到的是，我大概 2014 年搬来 Los Angeles，看到的那些开发项目——

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: You'd have a really exciting neighborhood.
turns.zh: 你会看到一个特别有意思的街区，

turns.en: Pop up in Silver Lake or Echo Park or Highland Park. And then whenever scaffolding would go up for a new building, there's generally a, oh, oh no, what's that going to be? And that's not the reaction that you should have when a new building is being built.
turns.zh: 在 Silver Lake、Echo Park 或者 Highland Park 冒出来。然后每当你看到一栋新楼搭起脚手架，大家的反应通常是'哦，哦不，那会是个什么东西？'而当一栋新楼要建起来时，你不该是这种反应。

turns.en: There should be some excitement. What is that going to be?
turns.zh: 应该有点兴奋感才对。那会是个什么东西？

turns.en: What kind of new creative spirit is going to enter into that structure? And I just don't think the commercial real estate industry is that inspiring in that way? Those outcomes haven't been so inspiring. So our goal is to sort of infuse development with the art spirit.
turns.zh: 会有什么样的新创意精神注入到那栋建筑里？我就是觉得商业地产行业在那方面没那么鼓舞人心，那些结果也一直没那么让人兴奋。所以我们的目标，就是把艺术精神注入到开发当中。

turns.en: I'm going to ask a very basic L.A. question, and I'd be curious to get both your takes on this. And again, Joe gave the caveat earlier, which is we've been to L.A. a couple of times, but we don't know that much about it. Whenever I come here, I am sort of stunned by the diversity of independent businesses compared.
turns.zh: 我要问一个非常基础的 L.A. 问题，也想听听你们俩的看法。Joe 前面也说过这个前提，就是我们来过 L.A. 几次，但对它了解不多。每次我来这儿，都有点被这里独立商户（independent businesses）的多样性震惊到，跟——

turns.en: To New York.
turns.zh: 跟 New York 比。

turns.en: I think about this all the time.
turns.zh: 我一直在想这个问题。

turns.en: Yeah, there's so many mom and pop shops.
turns.zh: 对，这里有太多夫妻小店（mom and pop shops）了。

turns.en: I passed by a linoleum emporium on the way over here, which I just don't think you would ever see in New York. And I'm sure the direction of travel for a lot of independent businesses isn't that great. But how have so many managed to survive in L.A. so far compared to other places in the U.S.
turns.zh: 我来的路上经过一家油毡大卖场（linoleum emporium），这种东西我觉得你在 New York 是永远看不到的。我相信很多独立商户的发展趋势并不太好。但跟美国其他地方比，为什么这么多独立商户至今还能在 L.A. 生存下来？

turns.en: Well, I went to school in New York, went to NYU, and a lot of my most talented friends left New York and moved to Los Angeles because New York just got too expensive and yeah LA it's it's while it's expensive to buy a home in LA you can generally find a good rental deal in a really exciting neighborhood um it's a lot harder to do that in New York City so you have people who are just dedicated to their craft who can survive in LA and focus on their art Versus in New York, it's a lot more difficult to be able to focus on your craft while being able to pay rent. So I think you just have more of an experimental group of people who are moving out here and who exist and trying to start and create new ideas.
turns.zh: 嗯，我在 New York 上的学，读的是 NYU，我很多最有才华的朋友都离开了 New York 搬到 Los Angeles，因为 New York 实在太贵了。是啊，L.A.，虽然在 L.A. 买房很贵，但你通常能在一个特别有意思的街区找到不错的租房价格，在 New York City 就难多了。所以你会看到一批一心扑在自己手艺上的人，他们能在 L.A. 活下去、专注于自己的艺术；而在 New York，一边付房租一边专注于手艺就要难得多。所以我觉得，搬来这儿、在这儿生存、尝试开创和创造新想法的人，是更偏实验性的一群。

turns.en: Bill, thoughts?
turns.zh: Bill，你怎么看？

turns.en: I would also address the density issue. In New York, you have really high density and therefore you're going to have high rent.
turns.zh: 我还想谈谈密度（density）的问题。在 New York，密度非常高，所以租金也会很高，

turns.en: For a particular location. Here we're really spread out.
turns.zh: 尤其是特定地段。而我们这儿是真的铺得很开。

turns.en: Yeah. which is an issue, by the way. We should address zoning in LA because we can't stay spread out forever or as spread out as we are. But I think that's a reason that you see so many mom and pop shops, which is great. In my community, I live right off PCH, Pacific Coast Highway, and most of the stores are mom and pops. There are some chain restaurants and stuff. So I think it's the density.
turns.zh: 对。顺便说一句，这本身就是个问题。我们应该处理一下 L.A. 的分区规划（zoning），因为我们不可能永远这么摊开、摊得这么开。但我觉得这正是你看到这么多夫妻小店的原因，这是好事。在我住的社区，我就住在 PCH，也就是 Pacific Coast Highway 旁边，大多数店铺都是夫妻店。也有一些连锁餐厅之类的。所以我觉得关键就在密度。

turns.en: That I have to say, I've talked about this.
turns.zh: 这一点我得说，我一直都在讲这个。

turns.en: I love strip malls.
turns.zh: 我超爱那种沿街商业街（strip malls）。

turns.en: I love seeing the Korean restaurant next to the tooth whitening place, next to the vape shop, next to the karate school.
turns.zh: 我就爱看那种韩国餐厅挨着牙齿美白店、挨着电子烟店、再挨着空手道学校的景象。

turns.en: To me, that's one of my faves. I love driving by.
turns.zh: 对我来说，那是我的最爱之一。我开车经过的时候特别享受。

turns.en: Truly multi-use development.
turns.zh: 这才是真正的多用途开发（multi-use development）。

turns.en: But Zach, when you're thinking about, okay, you want this to be, you want to create a building that actually get people excited rather than another building.
turns.zh: 但 Zach，当你在想，好，你想让这栋楼——你想建一栋真正能让人兴奋起来的楼，而不是又一栋普通的楼，

turns.en: What are the ingredients to that?
turns.zh: 那需要哪些要素？

turns.en: I think you have to be focused on, so the way that we're trying to approach finding tenants, we like to think of it like almost like how a 24 tries to find filmmakers.
turns.zh: 我觉得你得专注于——我们找租户（tenants）的方式，我们喜欢把它想成几乎就像 A24 找电影人那样。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: So how can we find someone who has a vision? We're not trying to find another Shake Shack.
turns.zh: 那我们怎么才能找到有愿景的人？我们不是要再找一家 Shake Shack。

turns.en: I mean, yeah. So Shake Shack is awesome.
turns.zh: 我是说，是啊，Shake Shack 很棒。

turns.en: I love going to Shake Shack when I'm at the airport, but I don't necessarily need Shake Shack everywhere else. So I think people get a lot more excited when people are trying new things and are trying to, to test the limits of even pastries, whatever it is, if you're passionate about a thing, then that passion usually translates into an exciting new result.
turns.zh: 我在机场的时候很爱去 Shake Shack，但我并不需要到处都有 Shake Shack。所以我觉得，当人们在尝试新东西、在试探极限——哪怕是糕点之类的，只要你对一件事有热情，那种热情通常就会转化成一个激动人心的新成果，人们就会兴奋得多。

turns.en: So that's how we approach trying to find tenants.
turns.zh: 这就是我们找租户的思路。

turns.en: How do you think about the trade-off, if there is one, between taste and, I guess, profitability? Because I think about A24. A24 makes a bunch of really good movies. There are a lot of good movies out there that don't necessarily make a lot of money. And unfortunately, some of the movies that make a lot of money are, you know, Marvel superhero things that are the same thing over and over as we were discussing with Hayes.
turns.zh: 你怎么看待品味（taste）和——我猜是盈利能力（profitability）之间的取舍，如果真有取舍的话？因为我会想到 A24。A24 做了一堆特别好的电影。市面上有很多好电影不一定赚很多钱。而不幸的是，一些赚大钱的电影，你懂的，就是那种 Marvel 超级英雄片，翻来覆去都是同一套，就像我们跟 Hayes 讨论时说的那样。

turns.en: But how do you.
turns.zh: 但你到底怎么

turns.en: Turn taste into actual profit when it comes to property?
turns.zh: 把品味变成实实在在的利润，在地产这行？

turns.en: Well, the lucky thing about real estate is even if the tenant fails, which is sad, but the real estate still maintains its value.
turns.zh: 嗯，房地产幸运的一点是，就算租户失败了——这当然很遗憾——但地产本身仍然保有其价值。

turns.en: And then a new tenant generally will come in.
turns.zh: 然后通常会有新租户进来。

turns.en: It's not like a movie where if no one sees the movie, you just write off the loss. So the real estate generally retains its value. even if there's a failure.
turns.zh: 它不像电影，如果没人看这部电影，你就直接把亏损核销掉。所以即便出现失败，房地产通常也能保住它的价值。

turns.en: Bill, you mentioned zoning.
turns.zh: Bill，你提到了分区规划。

turns.en: And one of the questions, you know, we've had a lot of conversations about zoning, but, you know, people fight about, oh, is this residential?
turns.zh: 其中一个问题是，你知道，我们聊过很多次分区规划了，但大家会争论，哦，这块是住宅用途吗？

turns.en: Is this business, et cetera? From your perspective, like.
turns.zh: 是商业用途等等？从你的角度看，

turns.en: When you think about we want to crack the puzzle, we want to make affordability, et cetera, we want this to be lively.
turns.zh: 当你想破解这个难题、想解决可负担性（affordability）等等、想让这里充满活力的时候，

turns.en: In your research, how important.
turns.zh: 在你的研究中，

turns.en: Is like getting that regulatory piece of the puzzle correct?
turns.zh: 把这块监管（regulatory）的拼图拼对有多重要？

turns.en: But if you talk to the home builders or the apartment builders, it's the biggest piece.
turns.zh: 但如果你去问那些住宅 builder 或者公寓 builder，这是最大的一块。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: So I think getting zoning changed. I mean, you know, we've passed some things in California. California has.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得推动分区规划改变——我是说，你知道，我们在 California 已经通过了一些东西。California 已经——

turns.en: But the ADU laws. Yeah.
turns.zh: 就是那些 ADU 法规。对。

turns.en: ADUs are really taking off in a lot of parts of California.
turns.zh: ADU（附属住宅单元，accessory dwelling unit）在 California 的很多地方正在真正火起来。

turns.en: Yeah. Now, the only problem is that's a.
turns.zh: 对。现在唯一的问题是，这只是对住房存量的一个

turns.en: Small increase to the housing stock. But, you know, actual zoning is really– changing zoning is really hard. You know, they have done some things like near transport centers you can build a lot higher density. One of the things that we're in an official housing crisis in California. So I think we're still in it. They announced it four or five years ago. And you weren't allowed to reduce density. So if you bought a six-unit apartment building, you couldn't build four condos. Or in my community, what was happening was... People with all kinds of money were buying two or three homes in a row and building a real mansion, not a McMansion.
turns.zh: 很小的增量。但你知道，真正的分区规划——改分区规划真的很难。他们确实做了一些事情，比如在交通中心附近你可以建得密度高很多。有一点是，我们正处于一场官方认定的住房危机中，在 California。所以我觉得我们还在这场危机里。他们四五年前就宣布了。而且当时不允许你降低密度。所以如果你买了一栋六户的公寓楼，你不能改建成四套公寓（condos）。或者在我住的社区，当时发生的情况是……各种有钱人连着买下两三套房子，然后建一栋真正的豪宅（mansion），不是那种暴发户式的大宅（McMansion）。

turns.en: And they've stopped that.
turns.zh: 然后他们把这种做法叫停了。

turns.en: Because density was actually decreasing in the beach communities, which.
turns.zh: 因为在那些海滨社区，密度实际上是在下降的，这

turns.en: You know, is kind of the opposite of what we kind of need.
turns.zh: 你知道，基本上跟我们需要的相反。

turns.en: And I'm speaking a little bit against my own interest in that because we'll have more traffic and stuff.
turns.zh: 而且我这么说其实有点违背我自己的利益，因为那样我们会有更多车流之类的。

turns.en: Thank you for your public interest.
turns.zh: 感谢你的公益之心。

turns.en: By the way, just to add to Zach's comment, when I'm talking with him, I think one of the things that really adds value to what he's doing is he's taking an area and building it into a community and making it kind of like you go into that community and it's like a symphony. And I thought it was an incredibly exciting idea to do. not just build one building, which is what a lot of people do, but they are taking multiple buildings and trying to build a whole community with new restaurants and a real vision for that. And I think that will have a real big impact.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，补充一下 Zach 的话，我跟他聊的时候，我觉得他做的事情里真正增值的一点，是他在把一片区域建成一个社区，让它有点像——你走进那个社区，就像走进一首交响乐。我觉得这是个极其令人兴奋的想法。不是只建一栋楼——很多人就是这么干的——而是他们在拿下多栋楼，试图建起一整个社区，配上新的餐厅，有一个真正的愿景。我觉得那会带来非常大的影响。

turns.en: Wait, Zach, say more about that. So what happens when you're buying multiple buildings in a single neighborhood and sort of aggregating those developments versus maybe just like cherry picking a few properties that are scattered across the city?
turns.zh: 等等，Zach，多说说这个。当你在同一个街区买下多栋楼、把这些开发项目聚合起来，跟也许只是在城市各处挑几个零散的物业相比，会发生什么？

turns.en: So yes, the idea for what we're doing on Western and Melrose came mostly from reading this book, The Death and Life of Great American Cities by Jane Jacobs. And she was talking about the sidewalk ballet in Greenwich Village. And growing up in New York City, I'd seen that firsthand. And Greenwich Village is one of the most exciting neighborhoods to just walk around and do nothing because you're experiencing culture by just existing. And that was the one thing I felt like was missing in Los Angeles. There are a few of these great main streets in LA, but there's very few. And generally when they exist, they end up sort of turning into airport shopping malls.
turns.zh: 是的，我们在 Western 和 Melrose 做的这个想法，主要来自读 Jane Jacobs 的那本书《美国大城市的死与生》（The Death and Life of Great American Cities）。她讲到了 Greenwich Village 的'人行道芭蕾'（sidewalk ballet）。我在 New York City 长大，亲眼见过。Greenwich Village 是最令人兴奋的街区之一，你就在那儿闲逛、什么都不干也很棒，因为你光是存在着就在体验文化。而这正是我觉得 Los Angeles 所缺的那样东西。L.A. 有几条这样很棒的主街，但非常少。而且通常当它们存在时，最后往往会变成机场式的购物中心。

turns.en: Eventually.
turns.zh: 最终。

turns.en: And that's just very disappointing because speaking of zoning, New York is basically all mixed use. So if there's a street, I mean, Manhattan at this point is so expensive that it's hard to have independent businesses. But for a while, even if there were a lot of chains on one street, you could go to a side street and see something interesting. LA doesn't have the luxury of doing that because roughly 95% of the city is residentially zoned.
turns.zh: 而这真的很让人失望，因为说到分区规划，New York 基本上全是混合用途（mixed use）。所以如果有一条街——我是说，Manhattan 现在贵到很难有独立商户了。但有一段时间，即便一条街上有很多连锁店，你也可以拐到旁边的小街看到有意思的东西。L.A. 没有这个余地，因为这座城市大约 95% 都是住宅分区（residentially zoned）。

turns.en: So if you have a community that.
turns.zh: 所以如果你有一个社区，

turns.en: Has their main street, have all of the culture and life taken out of it, then that's it.
turns.zh: 它的主街被抽走了所有的文化和生机，那就完了。

turns.en: You got nothing because it's just residential around you.
turns.zh: 你什么都没有，因为你周围全都是住宅。

turns.en: You know, sometimes there are these fights on Twitter where they talk about like, what are the best, most walkable cities? And it's like, oh, New York is very, very walkable. And then there's like, oh, LA is at the bottom. Except it's always so nice, the weather out here.
turns.zh: 你知道，Twitter 上有时候会有这种争论，聊哪些是最好、最适合步行的城市。就会有人说，哦，New York 非常非常适合步行。然后又有人说，哦，L.A. 排在最底部。可偏偏这儿的天气总是这么好。

turns.en: I don't mind walking an hour. So I'm actually totally fine.
turns.zh: 我不介意走一个小时。所以我其实完全没问题。

turns.en: I actually think LA is a great walking city because I never have to worry about the weather.
turns.zh: 我其实觉得 L.A. 是个很棒的步行城市，因为我从来不用担心天气。

turns.en: I think it's one of the most walkable cities. It's so pleasant to walk here. But can I... No, I love walking here. But it does not, I guess, suppose... You'll be walking for a long time.
turns.zh: 我觉得它是最适合步行的城市之一。在这儿走路太舒服了。但我能不能……不，我很爱在这儿走路。但它确实不，我猜，算是……你会走很长的路。

turns.en: Yeah, it's great.
turns.zh: 是啊，很棒。

turns.en: I love walking for a long time here, and I've taken many.
turns.zh: 我很爱在这儿走很长的路，我也走过很多

turns.en: Long walks in L.A., but I know it does not meet what most people are talking about when they say walkable.
turns.zh: 很长的路，在 L.A.，但我知道它并不符合大多数人说的'适合步行'的那个意思。

turns.en: Okay, you have this vision, this.
turns.zh: 好，你有这个愿景，这个

turns.en: Community, et cetera.
turns.zh: 社区等等。

turns.en: How much right now is your business being affected or how much when you're thinking about this, are you thinking about the headwinds.
turns.zh: 现在你的生意在多大程度上受到影响，或者说你在想这件事的时候，有多大会去想那些逆风（headwinds），

turns.en: That we talked about with Hayes right before it?
turns.zh: 就是我们在这期节目前面跟 Hayes 聊到的那些？

turns.en: The fact that there is this very.
turns.zh: 就是存在这么一个非常

turns.en: Big industry that is on the decline and how does that make you think about the business, the opportunity set?
turns.zh: 庞大的、正在走下坡路的行业这个事实，这如何影响你对这门生意、对机会集（opportunity set）的思考？

turns.en: So I think the commercial real estate industry is having a really tough time because for a long time we've been able to make money by financially engineering outcomes. And now the financial conditions are not super great for those financially engineered outcomes. You can't get a cap rate and an interest rate arbitrage and make money. You can't throw a bunch of people in a room of 140 IQ and do some spreadsheets and figure out how to make money when the interest rates are higher than what you bought the building for on a cap rate. So now you actually have to make the product good.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得商业地产行业现在日子很难过，因为长期以来我们都能靠金融工程（financial engineering）去操纵结果来赚钱。而现在，对于那些靠金融工程做出来的结果，金融环境并不太好。你没法再靠资本化率（cap rate）和利率之间的套利去赚钱了。你没法把一堆智商 140 的人塞进一个房间，做几张电子表格，就想出怎么在利率高于你买入这栋楼时的资本化率的情况下还能赚钱。所以现在你真的得把产品本身做好。

turns.en: I see what you're saying.
turns.zh: 我明白你的意思。

turns.en: And I think that's what's really exciting about what we're doing is we're seeing rents increase where we are because I think we've made a really exciting product by investing in talent. There's a lot of new apartment buildings in LA. I don't think many people go around going, wow, that's such a beautiful, cool new apartment building. I think most people are like, oh God, not another one of those boring, generic apartment buildings. So I think the commercial real estate industry, now we have to actually make good products if we want.
turns.zh: 我觉得这正是我们做的事情真正令人兴奋的地方——我们这边的租金在上涨，因为我觉得我们靠投资人才做出了一个特别有意思的产品。L.A. 有很多新公寓楼。我不觉得有多少人会在旁边走过然后感叹'哇，那栋新公寓楼真漂亮、真酷'。我觉得大多数人的反应是'天哪，又来一栋那种无聊、千篇一律的公寓楼'。所以我觉得，商业地产行业现在如果想

turns.en: To make money.
turns.zh: 赚钱，我们就真的得做出好产品。

turns.en: Okay, so speaking of making good products, I read one of the things you're doing as part of your developing is you're building city infrastructure as well. So installing things like crosswalks. What's the process of creating a crosswalk in LA?
turns.zh: 好，说到做好产品，我看到你们在开发过程中做的一件事，是你们还在建城市基础设施（city infrastructure）。比如安装人行横道（crosswalk）之类的东西。在 L.A. 建一个人行横道是个什么流程？

turns.en: It's like a Kafka novel. It's just horrible.
turns.zh: 就像一部 Kafka 的小说。简直糟糕透顶。

turns.en: Tell us more.
turns.zh: 多讲讲。

turns.en: Oh, we got a great email. We got approved for a crosswalk on Clinton and Western. And it said it'll be built in a few years or more.
turns.zh: 哦，我们收到一封很棒的邮件。我们申请在 Clinton 和 Western 路口建人行横道获批了。邮件上说，它会在几年或者更久之后建成。

turns.en: Wait, what's the constraint?
turns.zh: 等等，卡点在哪？

turns.en: Like what is the actual holdup? What's your sense of the holdup?
turns.zh: 到底耽搁在哪？你觉得耽搁的原因是什么？

turns.en: They, uh, there's no really process to get one. You can, you have to pay for it. That's they're like, Oh yeah, we'll, we'll totally approve that for you, but it's going to cost a million dollars. And then we're like, just to put a, stop like a light and they're like well the engineering the electrical and then you got to go put a vault underneath for us so it's like they're like what are you going to do for us interesting It's funny to think a few years are up. It reminds me of when I used to, as a young kid, like be a vinyl record collector and you'd see the 99 cents and up bins. And it's like, so this is the bin that contained, you could have a hundred dollar record in the 99 cents and up bins.
turns.zh: 他们，呃，其实根本没有一个真正的流程去拿到一个。你可以——你得自己掏钱。他们会说'哦是啊，我们当然可以批给你，但这要花一百万美元。'然后我们就说，就为了装一个——装个红绿灯而已，他们就说'好吧，工程、电气，然后你还得给我们在底下埋一个管线 vault。'所以就好像他们在说'你能为我们做点什么有意思的？'。想想挺好笑的，还要好几年。这让我想起小时候我收藏黑胶唱片，你会看到那种'99 美分及以上'的箱子。就是说，那个箱子里，你可能会在'99 美分及以上'的箱子里翻到一张一百美元的唱片。

turns.en: I'm curious, Bill, you talk to the home builders. Have they become more of the product mindset? Like, do they, are they going in the same direction where it's like, okay, it's not just good enough to have like a master plan community or something.
turns.zh: 我很好奇，Bill，你跟那些住宅 builder 打交道。他们有没有变得更注重产品思维？就是说，他们是不是也在往同一个方向走，觉得'好，光有一个总体规划社区（master plan community）之类的还不够，'

turns.en: We have to think about.
turns.zh: 我们得去思考

turns.en: The freestanding home as a desirable product rather than just a place to live.
turns.zh: 把这栋独立住宅当成一个有吸引力的产品，而不只是一个住的地方。

turns.en: Is that a thing yet?
turns.zh: 这种趋势出现了吗？

turns.en: Well, you know, most of the home builders that I speak to are infill builders. I do talk to some of the larger builders that the number one thing I've heard from them is they're concerned.
turns.zh: 嗯，你知道，我交流的大多数住宅 builder 都是填建型（infill）builder。我确实也跟一些更大的 builder 聊过，我从他们那儿听到的头号事情是他们在担心——

turns.en: They were really into the build to rent model. Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 他们之前特别热衷于建了用于出租（build-to-rent）的模式。是的，是的。

turns.en: And that's kind of under pressure right now. So as far as building a community, I still think they're sticking with their master plan.
turns.zh: 而这个模式现在有点承压。所以说到建社区，我仍然觉得他们还是坚持自己的总体规划。

turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.en: So it's interesting to hear him say that about the crosswalk because policy and zoning and regulatory issues are the number one thing I hear from home builders.
turns.zh: 所以听他讲人行横道那件事挺有意思的，因为政策、分区规划和监管问题，是我从住宅 builder 那儿听到的头号问题。

turns.en: They all feel right across. Of course, good times, bad times, that's always their number one issue.
turns.zh: 他们的感受完全一致。当然，好时候、坏时候，那永远都是他们的头号难题。

turns.en: I have another basic LA question. despite what Joe says about this being a walkable city, lots of people drive, right? Which means you have to have parking if you're doing a commercial development, right? Everyone needs to get there. And at the same time, I imagine having huge portions of the city as designated parking lots is not that attractive if you're trying to create a neighborhood or maybe even if you're trying to produce profit. How do you think about the trade-off between parking versus creating a beautiful neighborhood with many tasteful buildings?
turns.zh: 我还有一个基础的 L.A. 问题。尽管 Joe 说这是座适合步行的城市，还是有很多人开车，对吧？这意味着如果你做商业开发，你就得有停车场，对吧？每个人都得到得了那儿。同时我又觉得，如果你想打造一个街区、甚至如果你想创造利润的话，把城市里一大片一大片的地方划成停车场并不是那么有吸引力。你怎么看待'停车场'和'打造一个有很多有品位的楼、漂亮的街区'之间的取舍？

turns.en: It's definitely my biggest blind spot because I didn't drive for most of my life living in New York. So people who are from L.A. are always asking me what the parking situation is. And I'm like, why do you keep asking me about the parking? Don't you want to know what the restaurants are? And they're like, well, where am I going to park?
turns.zh: 这绝对是我最大的盲点，因为我在 New York 生活的大半辈子都没开过车。所以那些 L.A. 本地人总问我停车情况怎么样。我就说，你们怎么老问我停车的事？你们不想知道有哪些餐厅吗？他们就说，那我停哪儿啊？

turns.en: I had a friend. I have a friend from L.A. who will park.
turns.zh: 我有个朋友。我有个 L.A. 的朋友，他会停车，

turns.en: And then we're going half a block north and he'll get out, he'll drive his car and then park half a block north.
turns.zh: 然后我们要往北走半个街区，他会下车、把车开过去，再停在往北半个街区的地方。

turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: But no, it's a thing.
turns.zh: 但不，这是真事儿。

turns.en: It's a thing.
turns.zh: 这是真事儿。

turns.en: Especially if you have kids, like you got to get them in the car seats, get them out of the car seats. So if you can't park, it's like Fairfax is like just horrendous parking. And sometimes you'll just not go to the business if the parking's that bad.
turns.zh: 尤其是如果你有小孩，你得把他们塞进安全座椅、再抱出来。所以如果你没法停车——比如 Fairfax 的停车简直是灾难。有时候停车那么糟糕，你干脆就不去那家店了。

turns.en: But you can you can make it work with valet.
turns.zh: 但你可以靠代客泊车（valet）来解决。

turns.en: Let me add something here too. I mentioned the ADUs and that they have picked up a little bit. But one of the rules with the ADUs is you don't have to have off-street parking. So what's happening in a lot of the communities where they are building a lot of ADUs is the streets are just packed.
turns.zh: 我也补充一点。我提到 ADU，说它们有点起色了。但 ADU 的规则之一是，你不必配建街外停车位（off-street parking）。所以在很多大量建 ADU 的社区，正在发生的情况是，街道被塞得满满当当。

turns.en: So even worse than they were before.
turns.zh: 所以甚至比以前还糟。

turns.en: So parking, until we get real self-driving cars and nobody has to have a car anymore, parking is a huge issue.
turns.zh: 所以停车这件事，在我们真正用上自动驾驶汽车（self-driving cars）、没人再需要自己拥有一辆车之前，是个大问题。

turns.en: Koreatown. is one of the craziest parking situations, maybe on the planet.
turns.zh: Koreatown 是全世界——也许是这个星球上——最疯狂的停车局面之一。

turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。

turns.en: People will, there'll be no spots. My wife lived in Koreatown for a little while. And then there's people who are, like, just sitting there all day. And then once someone leaves, they're, like, coordinating how to get all the spots.
turns.zh: 人们会——一个车位都没有。我太太在 Koreatown 住过一阵子。然后就有人整天守在那儿。一旦有人开走，他们就开始协调怎么把那些车位都抢到。

turns.en: So Koreatown's pretty rough.
turns.zh: 所以 Koreatown 挺艰难的。

turns.en: But I do think with self-driving cars, parking will become less important.
turns.zh: 但我确实觉得，有了自动驾驶汽车，停车会变得更不重要。

turns.en: No, I'm fascinated by this question because it's like the car drives you to work and then goes to some centralized lot, like, I want to do like a bunch of episodes because it could just end up meaningfully restructuring cities and how they're organized.
turns.zh: 不，我对这个问题特别着迷，因为就好像车把你送到上班的地方，然后自己开到某个集中的停车场。我想做好几期节目聊这个，因为它最终可能实实在在地重构城市以及它们的组织方式。

turns.en: Let me just interrupt you quickly. It also would change the way houses look. Yeah, right.
turns.zh: 我打断你一下。它还会改变房子的样子。对，没错。

turns.en: Because right now in a lot of communities, you've got these garages in front and they're really ugly.
turns.zh: 因为现在很多社区里，你把车库建在前面，而且特别丑。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: You know, and it would be really nice if those all went away.
turns.zh: 你知道，如果那些车库全都消失，那会特别好。

turns.en: And my brother pointed out to me one of the biggest changes, of course, would be self-driving would be.
turns.zh: 我兄弟还跟我指出，最大的变化之一，当然，自动驾驶带来的会是——

turns.en: Police interactions go way down.
turns.zh: 跟警察打交道的次数大幅减少。

turns.en: Yes, right.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.en: It also means lower speeding ticket revenue. There are all kinds of, there are going to be no speeding tickets anymore, which is going to hurt.
turns.zh: 这也意味着超速罚单收入下降。会有各种——以后不会再有超速罚单了，这会让（政府收入）受损。

turns.en: I hope this happens in my lifetime.
turns.zh: 我希望这能在我有生之年实现。

turns.en: I have a question, you know, this is a question that I probably would have asked very first off in like 2021 or 2022, then it faded.
turns.zh: 我有个问题，你知道，这个问题我在 2021 或 2022 年大概会一上来就问，后来它慢慢淡出了。

turns.en: But I'm curious now, how hard is it to like.
turns.zh: 但我现在很好奇，比如

turns.en: Find construction materials or like HVAC things or all or the electricity transformers yeah like because what now we know there's incredible competition for a lot of that stuff is that showing up in your development timelines transformers yeah so what's.
turns.zh: 去找建筑材料，或者暖通空调（HVAC）设备，或者电力变压器（transformers）之类的有多难，因为现在我们知道那很多东西竞争都极其激烈，这会体现在你的开发时间表里吗？变压器，是的，那么

turns.en: Happening up with that you got to fight for it yeah yeah what does.
turns.zh: 现在是什么情况？你得去抢。是的，是的。这到底

turns.en: That actually mean though do you pay a higher price or do you I don't everyone always talks about building the relationship with the supplier do you become their best friend how does fight for it.
turns.zh: 是什么意思呢？你是付更高的价钱，还是——我不确定——大家总说要跟供应商搞好关系，你要变成他们最好的朋友吗？'去抢'到底是怎么个抢法？

turns.en: Mean Yeah, you got to find a guy who knows a guy.
turns.zh: 意思是啊，你得找到一个'认识某个人的那个人'。

turns.en: Find the guy.
turns.zh: 找到那个人。

turns.en: And then you got to buy it in advance and then store it somewhere.
turns.zh: 然后你得提前买下来，再找个地方存着。

turns.en: Huh.
turns.zh: 哈。

turns.en: Yeah, it's like, yeah, it gets weird.
turns.zh: 是啊，就像，是的，会变得很诡异。

turns.en: So do you have a garage just like full of Transformers somewhere?
turns.zh: 所以你是不是在某个地方有个车库，里面塞满了变压器？

turns.en: I might.
turns.zh: 可能有。

turns.en: No, like when you were like. It's a very valuable.
turns.zh: 不，就像你刚才说的。这可是很值钱的。

turns.en: Tracy's going to add that to her prepper. I probably will. As my fellow prepper, yeah, got to have a garage full of Transformers.
turns.zh: Tracy 要把这个加进她的'末日准备'（prepper）清单了。我大概会。作为同为末日准备者（fellow prepper）的伙伴，是啊，得有一个塞满变压器的车库。

turns.en: Got to do it together.
turns.zh: 得一起干。

turns.en: Long term, people are always going to love living around here.
turns.zh: 长远看，人们永远会喜欢住在这附近。

turns.en: We can talk about Hollywood, sure, but this is heaven on earth here.
turns.zh: 我们当然可以聊 Hollywood，但这里就是人间天堂。

turns.en: This is God's country.
turns.zh: 这是上帝眷顾之地。

turns.en: In the end, it's.
turns.zh: 到头来，它

turns.en: Always going to be great, right?
turns.zh: 永远都会很棒，对吧？

turns.en: That's my.
turns.zh: 这就是我的

turns.en: L.A.
turns.zh: L.A.

turns.en: Take.
turns.zh: 看法。

turns.en: I think Los Angeles has the highest ceiling of any city in the world.
turns.zh: 我觉得 Los Angeles 拥有世界上所有城市里最高的上限。

turns.en: I completely agree. I'm such an L.A.
turns.zh: 我完全同意。我真是个 L.A.（拥趸）。

turns.en: We have two problems. One is the cost of housing, which we need to address, and the other is water.
turns.zh: 我们有两个问题。一个是住房成本，这是我们需要解决的；另一个是水。

turns.en: Water in California is a huge, huge issue.
turns.zh: 水在 California 是一个巨大、巨大的问题。

turns.en: Another topic we could talk for a long time, but Bill and Zach, thank you so much for joining us at OzLots Live.
turns.zh: 这又是一个我们能聊很久的话题，但 Bill 和 Zach，非常感谢你们来到 Odd Lots Live 现场。

turns.en: We really appreciate you and both of you.
turns.zh: 我们真的很感谢你们两位。

turns.zh: 谢谢。
